Pharmacological Management of Pain Disorders

Opioids, non-opioid analgesics, NSAIDs, local anesthetics, topicals, and antispasmodics — mechanisms, adverse effects, and how to choose an agent across acute, obstetric, and chronic pain.

PLO 1

Pain Disorders and Etiologies

Acute vs. Chronic Pain

The very first branch point in any pain question — on an exam or in clinic — is duration. Everything downstream (which drug class, how aggressive to be, whether an opioid is ever reasonable) flows from this distinction.

⏱️

Acute Pain — <3 months

  • Injury, post-surgical, dental
  • Surgery
  • Obstetrics (labor & delivery)
  • Mucous membrane pain (pharyngitis, hemorrhoids)
  • Myocardial infarction
  • Non-low back soft tissue musculoskeletal injury
  • Low back pain
  • Headache
📅

Chronic Pain — >3 months

  • Osteoarthritis
  • Generalized pain (e.g. fibromyalgia)
  • Neuropathic: trigeminal neuralgia, diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia
  • Low back pain
  • Cancer pain
  • Headache
🔑 Why duration matters so much

The same complaint (e.g. low back pain) is managed completely differently depending on whether it's acute or chronic. Acute low back pain still gets an NSAID first-line; chronic low back pain also starts with an NSAID but opioids essentially never belong in the chronic plan, and second/third-line options shift toward antidepressants and gabapentinoids rather than muscle relaxants.

Six drug categories are used across these pain states — this notes file follows the same order as lecture:

1

Opioids

Potent & moderate μ-agonists, mixed agonist-antagonists — for moderate-severe pain.

2

Non-Opioid Analgesics

Acetaminophen, suzetrigine, antiepileptics, antidepressants.

3

NSAIDs

COX inhibitors — first-line for inflammatory and most musculoskeletal pain.

4

Local Anesthetics

Na⁺ channel blockers — topical, infiltration, nerve block, neuraxial.

5

Topicals

NSAIDs, capsaicin, menthol — site-directed with lower systemic exposure.

6

Antispasmodics

Centrally-acting muscle relaxants — adjuncts, never first-line.

Q: A patient reports low back pain that has been present for 4 months. Does this change your first-line agent choice compared to a patient with back pain for 2 weeks?

Answer

Not the first-line agent (NSAIDs are first-line in both), but it changes everything else: chronic pain shouldn't default to antispasmodics or opioids, non-pharmacologic measures become the primary treatment, and if a drug is added beyond NSAIDs, an SNRI (duloxetine) is preferred over anything sedating or habit-forming.

Drugs Used for Pain Management

Opioids

Opioids are organized by how strongly and reliably they activate the μ-opioid receptor. Potent full agonists are for severe pain; moderate agonists are submaximal and combined with an NSAID or acetaminophen; mixed agonist-antagonists behave differently depending on what else is on board.

Potent μ-Opioid Receptor Agonists (Schedule II)

Morphine, fentanyl, meperidine, methadone, and oxycodone — generally indicated for severe pain.

Morphine

PO / IV — reference standard

Considerable first-pass metabolism → larger PO doses needed vs. IV. Metabolites: 3-glucuronide (inactive) and 6-glucuronide (active). Indications: severe pain from trauma, MI, cancer, postsurgical pain. Sustained/extended-release useful in chronic pain.

Fentanyl Family

Injection, transdermal patch, lozenge, nasal spray

Family also includes sufentanil, remifentanil, alfentanil — highly potent, mainly anesthesia adjuncts. Fentanyl patch = long-acting, for chronic pain only. Lozenges/nasal spray = breakthrough pain.

Meperidine

Synthetic phenylpiperidine

Structurally unrelated to morphine. Poor oral bioavailability (300 mg PO ≈ 75 mg IV). Obstetric analgesic, short-term acute pain, and postoperative shivering (κ-receptor activity).

Methadone

Phenylheptylamine — long t½ 12–40 h

Also an NMDA-receptor antagonist and inhibits SERT (± NET) — may explain efficacy in neuropathic/cancer pain refractory to morphine. Used for chronic pain and opioid dependence (reduces craving without euphoria).

Oxycodone

Semisynthetic morphine derivative

Forms: single-agent SR (Oxycontin), + APAP (Percocet), + NSAID (Combunox). Metabolized via CYP2D6 & 3A4.

⚠️ Fentanyl patch — heat and naïve-patient warnings

Avoid exposing the patch site to external heat (heating pads, saunas, hot tubs, sunbathing) — at 40°C, serum fentanyl can increase by roughly one-third. Never use a fentanyl patch in an opioid-naïve patient, and dispose of used patches/lozenges properly (remaining drug is enough to harm a child or pet).

⚠️ Meperidine — normeperidine toxicity

Meperidine is metabolized to normeperidine, a toxic metabolite that causes CNS excitation and seizures. Do not use in the elderly or in renal impairment (normeperidine accumulates). Also has significant antimuscarinic effects and inhibits DAT/NET.

☐ Methadone Safety

Do not use in opioid-naïve patients. Lipophilic with a long and unpredictable half-life (12–40 h) — accumulation leads to toxicity. High doses (~200 mg/day) have been associated with torsade de pointes from QT prolongation.

⚠️ Oxycodone SR — crushed tablets

Ingestion of crushed sustained-release oxycodone tablets (defeating the SR mechanism → immediate full-dose release) has been implicated in many overdose deaths.

Moderate Opioid Agonists

Hydrocodone (CII) and codeine (CII–V) do not produce maximal analgesia at doses patients can tolerate — used at submaximal doses, usually combined with an NSAID or acetaminophen. Indicated for mild-to-moderate pain or as antitussives.

Hydrocodone

Semisynthetic analog of codeine

Metabolized via CYP2D6. Forms: extended-release capsule, fixed-dose combos (Lortab, Norco, Vicoprofen).

Codeine

Naturally occurring opiate, 3-O-methylmorphine

Metabolized to morphine by CYP2D6 (morphine is 200× more potent at the μ-receptor). Analgesic potency ~30% of morphine. Enzyme variants → inadequate relief (poor metabolizers) or toxicity (ultra-rapid metabolizers).

Tramadol (Ultram/Ultracet) & Tapentadol (Nucynta)

Dual-action analgesics

Both are μ-agonists that also inhibit norepinephrine reuptake; tramadol additionally inhibits serotonin reuptake. Indicated for moderate-severe pain and may help neuropathic pain. Tramadol is less effective than NSAIDs and has more adverse events.

⚠️ Tramadol — seizures & serotonin syndrome

Toxicity is associated with seizures — relative contraindication in seizure disorder. Risk of serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs (antidepressants, linezolid, St. John's wort) or CYP2D6-inhibiting drugs (e.g. fluoxetine blocks conversion of tramadol to its active metabolite, reducing efficacy while increasing serotonergic AEs).

Mixed Opioid Agonist-Antagonists (FYI)

Buprenorphine

Belbuca (buccal), Butrans (patch), Brixadi/Sublocade (SQ), SL tablet

Long-acting μ partial agonist with very high receptor affinity; antagonist at κ and δ receptors. Suboxone = buprenorphine + naloxone (naloxone blocks IV abuse). Replaces a shorter-acting, more abusable opioid with a longer-acting partial agonist in OUD treatment.

Butorphanol, Nalbuphine, Pentazocine

Mu-antagonist / kappa-agonist mixed agents

In opioid-naïve patients, act as agonists. In the presence of a full μ-agonist, all four drugs act as antagonists at the μ-receptor — hence "mixed agonist-antagonist." In opioid dependence, this blocking activity may precipitate withdrawal.

💡 Benefits vs. potential AEs (vs. a pure agonist)

Benefits: less respiratory depression, lower dependence/abuse potential, less constipation. Potential AEs: psychotomimetic effects (hallucinations), withdrawal precipitation. Indications: moderate-severe pain, pre/postoperative and obstetric analgesia; nasal butorphanol for migraine (last resort); buprenorphine specifically for opioid use disorder.

Relative Potency at the μ-Receptor

Potency can be estimated from equianalgesic parenteral doses (morphine 10 mg IM/IV = reference point):

Fentanyl — ~100×
Buprenorphine — ~33×
Oxymorphone — ~10×
Hydromorphone — ~6.7×
Morphine — 1× (reference) / Oxycodone — ~1×
Codeine / Meperidine / Tramadol — ~0.1×

Allergic Reactions

True allergy is rare — most "allergic" reactions are pruritus/flushing from direct mast cell histamine release, not IgE-mediated. For a genuine allergic reaction, switch to an opioid from a different chemical class:

MorphineMeperidine

Opioid Drug Interactions

Drug GroupInteraction with Opioids
Sedative-hypnoticsIncreased CNS depression, particularly respiratory depression
Antipsychotic tranquilizersIncreased sedation; variable effects on respiratory depression; accentuation of CV effects (antimuscarinic and α-blocking actions)
Monoamine oxidase inhibitorsRelative contraindication to all opioid analgesics due to high incidence of hyperpyrexic coma; hypertension also reported

Opioid Use — General Recommendations

✅ Acute Pain
  • For moderate acute pain not relieved by NSAID or NSAID/APAP combination
  • Most evidence: NSAIDs are as effective or more effective than opioids for acute pain, including low back pain
  • For severe pain (injury, trauma, post-surgical): immediate-release opioid at the lowest effective dose, shortest duration — do not use extended-release for acute pain
  • Prescribe PRN, not around-the-clock
  • Combine with a non-opioid (monitor total APAP dose)
🚫 Chronic Pain
  • NOT recommended first-line for chronic noncancer pain; use lowest dose and monitor for risk
  • Consider buprenorphine-based products for patients with OUD
  • Avoid multiple opioid therapies; use a controlled substance agreement
  • If used for neuropathic pain, use tramadol/tapentadol
  • DOC for cancer pain
  • Taper slowly when discontinuing to prevent withdrawal

Risk of Chronic Opioid Use

  • Constipation — most common AE; may require chronic laxative use
  • Depression — psychiatric comorbidities common with long-term use
  • Hormonal dysregulation — ↓ testosterone/estradiol → sexual dysfunction, infertility
  • Opioid-induced hyperalgesia
  • Opioid use disorder — withdrawal complicates discontinuation
  • Overdose — co-prescribe naloxone
☐ Opioids in Pregnancy & Lactation

All opioids are contraindicated for prolonged periods or high doses at term (this does not include opioids used for epidural/CSE/DPE). Associated with preterm delivery, poor fetal growth, stillbirth, birth defects (neural tube defects, congenital heart defects, gastroschisis), poor physiologic development, neurodevelopmental disorders, and neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome. Opioids also transfer into breast milk — a documented 2011 case involved an infant death from morphine toxicity after maternal opioid use during lactation, underscoring that lactation is not automatically "safe" from systemic opioid exposure.

Q: A patient with a documented true allergy to morphine needs an opioid for severe post-surgical pain. Which class should you choose from, and why?

Answer

Choose a phenylpiperidine (e.g. fentanyl) rather than another phenanthrene. Morphine is a phenanthrene; cross-reactivity is more likely within the same chemical class, so switching classes reduces the risk of a repeat reaction.

Drugs Used for Pain Management

Non-Opioid Analgesics

Acetaminophen, suzetrigine, antiepileptics, and antidepressants — a mixed-mechanism group united by not acting at the opioid receptor.

Acetaminophen (APAP)

Acetaminophen metabolism — glucuronidation and sulfation (nontoxic) vs. CYP2E1/3A4 oxidation to NAPQI (toxic, normally quenched by glutathione)

  • MOA: weak COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor in peripheral tissues; reduces fever by inhibiting prostaglandin formation/release in the CNS (non-selective CNS COX inhibitor; potentially inhibits COX-3)
  • Metabolite AM404 may act as a weak agonist at CB1/CB2 receptors
  • Minimal peripheral effect limits usefulness for peripheral inflammation
  • Pharmacokinetics: hepatic conjugation (sulfate, glucuronide); some CYP-mediated N-hydroxylation; metabolites renally excreted
⚠️ Hepatotoxicity

CYP2E1 oxidation forms NAPQI, which depletes glutathione and causes mitochondrial damage/hepatic cell death once GSH is exhausted. Do not exceed 4 g/day; max 2–3 g/day with chronic liver impairment. Chronic use increases toxicity; ethanol potentiates liver toxicity. Possible renal toxicity with long-term use of very large doses.

🔑 No longer automatic DOC for osteoarthritis

Per 2019 ACR guidelines, APAP is no longer the default for most OA patients — it's conditionally recommended only for mild OA when oral/topical NSAIDs aren't options or haven't helped, with close LFT monitoring. Meta-analyses suggest APAP monotherapy may be no better than placebo long-term.

✅ Pregnancy

APAP is safe when used as directed and is the preferred agent for most acute and chronic pain that is mild-to-moderate. No demonstrated association between prenatal acetaminophen exposure and child neurodevelopmental disorders in recent systematic review/meta-analysis data.

Suzetrigine (Journavx)

First-in-Class Non-Opioid NaV1.8 Inhibitor

MOA: selectively inhibits NaV1.8 channels — a voltage-gated sodium channel predominantly in peripheral nociceptive neurons of the dorsal root ganglia. Binds voltage-sensing domain 2 with an allosteric mechanism that stabilizes the closed state, causing tonic inhibition.

  • Indication: moderate-to-severe acute pain (not first-line — may not outperform ibuprofen/APAP)
  • PK: metabolized by CYP3A4 and induces CYP3A4
  • AEs: pruritus, rash, muscle spasms, ↑ creatine kinase
  • No addiction/dependence signal in human or animal studies so far
  • DDIs: contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and certain progestin-containing oral contraceptives
  • Pregnancy: animal studies demonstrated fetal harm

Antiepileptic Drugs

Useful for pain with an intermittent lancinating or continuous burning neuropathic quality: trigeminal neuralgia, postherpetic neuralgia, peripheral neuropathy. MOA is not fully clear — possibly inhibit conduction of pain impulses.

Carbamazepine

DOC for trigeminal neuralgia

MOA: blocks voltage-sensitive Na⁺ channels. Also used for partial/generalized tonic-clonic seizures and bipolar disorder. AEs: drowsiness, ataxia, mild leukopenia, hyponatremia, thrombocytopenia (high doses).

Gabapentinoids — Gabapentin & Pregabalin

Structural GABA analogs (not GABAergic in action)

No meaningful GABA-receptor activity. Inhibit presynaptic N-type Ca²⁺ channels by binding the α2δ1/α2δ2 accessory subunits, reducing excitatory neurotransmitter release. Indications: postherpetic neuralgia, seizures, fibromyalgia, neuropathic pain, restless leg syndrome, anxiety disorders.

☐ Carbamazepine — Serious Risks

Rare but serious: aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (10-fold higher incidence in East Asian descent — test for HLA-B*1502 before initiating), hepatic failure, pancreatitis. Pregnancy: 1st-trimester exposure increases risk of neural tube defects, craniofacial defects, fingernail hyperplasia, and developmental delay.

⚠️ Gabapentinoids — AEs, scheduling, and abuse potential

AEs: dizziness, drowsiness, ataxia, tremor, weight gain (especially pregabalin). Adjust dose in renal impairment. Tolerance and withdrawal seen with prolonged use — taper. Increasing concern for recreational use: pregabalin is Schedule V federally; gabapentin is unscheduled by the FDA but some states (not Maine) have scheduled it — Maine still requires PMP tracking.

Antidepressants

Useful in chronic pain syndromes: peripheral neuropathy, fibromyalgia, postherpetic neuralgia, migraine prophylaxis.

Amitriptyline

Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA)

Nonselective SERT/NET inhibition ↑ synaptic monoamines. Also antagonizes 5HT2A/5HT2C, muscarinic, α1, and histamine receptors, and inhibits voltage-gated Na⁺/K⁺ channels. AEs: anticholinergic (constipation, dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention), dizziness, weight gain, orthostatic hypotension. Cardiotoxic in overdose from ion channel inhibition.

Duloxetine (Cymbalta)

SNRI

Inhibits SERT and NET with no significant activity at other receptors — a "cleaner" side-effect profile than TCAs. AEs: nausea, diarrhea, cramping, rare hepatotoxicity.

Milnacipran (Savella)

SNRI

Antidepressant properties, but indicated specifically for fibromyalgia.

Q: A patient with postherpetic neuralgia is switched from gabapentin (ineffective, poorly tolerated) to an alternative. Which two drug classes are the standard next options, and how do you choose between them?

Answer

TCAs (amitriptyline) or another gabapentinoid (pregabalin) are standard alternatives. In general, if the pain is constant/burning, favor a TCA; if it's brief, recurrent, electric/lancinating, favor a gabapentinoid — and if one class fails, flip to the other.

Drugs Used for Pain Management

Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs)

  • Aspirin inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 irreversibly; anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antipyretic effects from nonspecific COX inhibition in peripheral tissues and CNS
  • All other NSAIDs are reversible inhibitors; most are nonselective COX inhibitors
  • "COX-2 inhibitors" are 8- to 25-fold more selective for COX-2 relative to COX-1
  • NSAIDs are superior to opioids for pain in which inflammation is involved

Propionic Acid Derivatives

Ibuprofen†, Naproxen†, Ketoprofen, Flurbiprofen, Oxaprozin

†Among the most widely used NSAIDs for pain/inflammation from trauma, infection, autoimmunity, neoplasm, joint degeneration. All reversibly and non-selectively inhibit COX. AEs: GI disturbance, peptic ulcer, liver/kidney injury.

Acetic Acid Derivatives

Indomethacin, Sulindac, Etodolac‡, Diclofenac, Ketorolac

‡Etodolac is relatively selective for COX-2. All reversibly/non-selectively inhibit COX otherwise.

Oxicams & Ketones

Piroxicam, Meloxicam*, Nabumetone

*Meloxicam is selective for COX-2 at low therapeutic doses.

Celecoxib (Celebrex)

Marketed COX-2 inhibitor

Anti-inflammatory/antipyretic/analgesic similar to traditional NSAIDs. Indications: OA, RA, JRA, acute pain, ankylosing spondylitis, primary dysmenorrhea. AEs: no antiplatelet action, ~20% ↓ GI bleeding vs. traditional NSAIDs, same renal effects.

💡 Why COX-2 selectivity raises CV risk

COX-2 inhibition ↓ prostacyclin → ↓ vasodilation and ↓ platelet inhibition. Because there's no COX-1 inhibition, there's no counterbalancing inhibition of vasoconstriction or platelet aggregation (no TXA2 blockade). Net result: increased thrombogenesis — this is the mechanistic basis for celecoxib's (and other selective COX-2 inhibitors') cardiovascular risk.

General Indications

  • Mild-to-moderate pain, headache, sports injuries, dysmenorrhea
  • Osteoarthritis; rheumatoid arthritis (usually with other therapies)
  • Bone pain in cancer patients

Precautions and Contraindications

Risk ProfileRecommended Approach
CV diseaseConsider a nonacetylated salicylate (diflunisal, salsalate, choline magnesium trisalicylate)
Low GI risk, high CV riskLower doses of naproxen
High GI risk, low CV riskCelecoxib or ibuprofen
High GI risk and high CV riskAvoid all NSAIDs, including celecoxib
Renal impairmentUse caution with any NSAID

SORT: Key Recommendations for Practice

Clinical RecommendationEvidence Rating
Knee/hand OA: topical NSAID first-line, then oral NSAID or duloxetine; hip OA similarly, but lacks topical evidenceA
Chronic low back pain: prefer topical/oral NSAIDs and SNRIsB
Chronic low back pain: avoid antiepileptics/gabapentinoids — no benefit, associated harmsB
Neuropathic pain: gabapentin, pregabalin, or duloxetineA
Fibromyalgia: pregabalin if tolerated, or duloxetine/milnacipranB
SNRIs (duloxetine, milnacipran) for fibromyalgia, neuropathic pain, and topical NSAIDs for chronic musculoskeletal painA

A = consistent, good-quality patient-oriented evidence; B = inconsistent or limited-quality evidence.

☐ NSAIDs in Pregnancy

≤20 weeks, if APAP is ineffective: NSAID use is reasonable. >20 to ≤28 weeks: short-term use (≤48 h) is reasonable — weigh risk vs. benefit against no analgesic or an opioid. Risk of fetal renal dysfunction, oligohydramnios, neonatal renal impairment. >28 weeks: use an opioid instead of an NSAID. NSAIDs should be avoided after 30 weeks — risk of premature closure of the ductus arteriosus → primary pulmonary hypertension of the newborn.

Q: A patient has a history of GI bleed and no cardiovascular disease. Which NSAID(s) fit this risk profile best?

Answer

High GI risk, low CV risk → celecoxib or ibuprofen are reasonable choices. If the patient instead had high CV risk with only low GI risk, lower-dose naproxen would be preferred; if both risks were high, NSAIDs (including celecoxib) should be avoided altogether.

Drugs Used for Pain Management

Local Anesthetics

Mechanism of Action

  • Local anesthetics (LAs) bind voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, which exist in 3 states: resting/closed, open, and inactivated
  • LAs have higher affinity for open and inactivated channels than for resting channels
  • LAs lengthen the "refractory period," preventing the channel from returning to resting/activatable state

Na⁺ channel conformational states — local anesthetics preferentially stabilize the open/inactivated states and prolong the refractory period

💡 Why this makes LAs selective for rapidly-firing neurons

Because the channel must already be open or inactivated for high-affinity binding, LAs work best on sensory neurons that are firing rapidly. To reach that binding site, the drug must first cross the membrane and get inside the nerve — which requires the uncharged (deprotonated) form, since these are weak bases governed by Henderson-Hasselbalch. But once inside, it needs to become charged (protonated) to bind the channel with any potency — this is why benzocaine (pKa 3.5, always uncharged, gets in easily) is actually a very weak anesthetic: it can't reprotonate to bind effectively.

Adjuncts

Sodium Bicarbonate

Co-injected with the LA to raise local pH, which shifts more of the weak-base drug to its uncharged form — increasing the rate of membrane penetration and therefore the rate of onset.

Epinephrine

Vasoconstriction maintains higher local drug concentration at the nerve (↑ duration) and reduces systemic absorption (↓ toxicity risk).

⚠️ Epinephrine — not for the extremities

AEs: tissue necrosis and hypoxia in areas with reduced blood flow. Epinephrine is not recommended in the extremities (fingers, toes, nose, ears, penis) — excessive vasoconstriction in an end-arterial supply risks ischemia.

Pharmacokinetics — Esters vs. Amides

🔑 Spelling mnemonic

Esters are spelled with one "i"; amides are spelled with two "i"s — a reliable way to sort any local anesthetic name you encounter.

Esters

Procaine, chloroprocaine, tetracaine, benzocaine, cocaine

  • Metabolized rapidly by plasma butyrylcholinesterase
  • One metabolite is para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) — excludes cocaine
  • PABA is the source of rare hypersensitivity to ester LAs (no cross-sensitivity between classes)

Amides

Lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine

  • Metabolized hepatically, primarily by CYP450 enzymes
  • True amide allergy is very rare
  • Preservatives in either class can resemble PABA and trigger a reaction independent of the anesthetic itself

Representative Uses by Drug

DrugClassTypical Clinical Use
LidocaineAmideTopical, infiltration, PNB, epidural, spinal — most versatile agent
BupivacaineAmidePNB, epidural, spinal — long duration, higher cardiotoxicity risk
RopivacaineAmidePNB, epidural — similar profile to bupivacaine, slightly less cardiotoxic
MepivacaineAmideInfiltration, PNB, epidural
PrilocaineAmideInfiltration; component of EMLA (risk of methemoglobinemia via o-toluidine metabolite)
ChloroprocaineEsterEpidural — fast onset, very short duration, low LAST risk
TetracaineEsterSpinal, topical — high potency, limited other use given LAST risk
ProcaineEsterSpinal
BenzocaineEsterTopical only — weak anesthetic despite easy membrane penetration
CocaineEster (atypical)Topical, ENT procedures — unique vasoconstrictor properties

Topical Combinations & Additional Topical Anesthetics

EMLA — Eutectic Mixture of Local Anesthetics

Combines lidocaine + prilocaine (both amides — no ester-allergy concern). A eutectic mixture is when two solids combine to form a liquid. Available as cream and patch; used for suturing, lumbar puncture, and numbing before needle sticks — especially valuable in pediatrics.

  • TAC (tetracaine–adrenaline–cocaine) and XAP (Xylocaine–adrenaline–Pontocaine) — non-commercial pharmacy-compounded mixtures, often used for facial laceration repair in children
  • Dyclonine — throat lozenges/sprays; Dibucaine — topical hemorrhoid preparations; Pramoxine — anesthetic/antipruritic for hemorrhoids, sunburn, itch preparations

Adverse Effects and Toxicity

  • Skeletal muscle tissue damage with improper/excess infiltration
  • All local anesthetics cause vasodilation except cocaine, which is a sympathomimetic (inhibits NET) and instead causes vasoconstriction

Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST)

Usually limited by minimizing systemic absorption. Risk correlates with potency:

Bupivacaine — highest cardiotoxicity
Ropivacaine — intermediate
Lidocaine — lowest cardiotoxicity
💡 CC:CNS ratio — margin of safety

The cardiovascular-collapse-to-CNS-toxicity dose ratio (CC:CNS) predicts margin of safety. Lidocaine > ropivacaine > bupivacaine for this ratio — a higher ratio means CNS symptoms (agitation, tinnitus) appear well before the cardiotoxic dose, giving a warning window to intervene. Lidocaine and mepivacaine primarily impair contractility; bupivacaine and ropivacaine primarily cause arrhythmias — the bigger concern with those two agents. LAST is uncommon with chloroprocaine due to its short duration of action.

Risk FactorsCNS Signs/SymptomsCardiovascular Signs/Symptoms
Unintended intravascular injection; extremes of age (<4 mo or >79 y); cardiac conduction/ischemic heart disease; renal/hepatic dysfunction; pregnancy; carnitine deficiency; highly vascular block siteTinnitus, circumoral numbness, metallic taste, agitation, dysarthria, seizures, loss of consciousnessHypotension, bradycardia, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiovascular collapse

LAST can occur >15 minutes after LA injection — delayed presentation is possible, not just immediate.

☐ Management of LAST

Provide ACLS measures (slightly modified — reduce epinephrine boluses to ≤1 mcg/kg, avoid vasopressin/calcium channel blockers/beta blockers/more LA, use amiodarone first-line). Benzodiazepines for seizures. Infuse 20% lipid emulsion — the antidote. Propofol is NOT a substitute for lipid emulsion, even though it's also lipid-formulated — do not use it in place of the actual lipid emulsion antidote.

Uses of Local Anesthetics

1

Topical Anesthesia

Short-term relief for mucous membrane or skin.

2

Infiltration Anesthesia

Injected intradermally/subcutaneously to numb an area — common in dentistry.

3

Peripheral Nerve Block

Percutaneous injection near a target nerve — minor (radial nerve) or major (brachial plexus).

4

Neuraxial Anesthesia

Injected near the spinal cord: epidural, CSE, DPE, spinal. Must be preservative-free.

Neuraxial anatomy — epidural, spinal, and caudal needle placement relative to the dura and subarachnoid space

✅ Regional Anesthesia (Bier's Block)

The extremity is isolated with a double tourniquet and LA is injected into a vein of that limb, anesthetizing the whole limb — used for short-duration (30–45 min) arm or hand surgery.

⚠️ Local Anesthetics in Pregnancy

Increased risk of LAST due to increased sensitivity to LA-induced cardiotoxicity and reduced serum levels of LA-binding proteins — a particular concern for blocks in highly vascular sites or requiring high LA volumes.

Q: A patient develops agitation and tinnitus 10 minutes after a peripheral nerve block with bupivacaine. What should you be worried about next, and what is the antidote if it progresses?

Answer

This is early LAST (CNS phase). Because bupivacaine has the highest cardiotoxicity of the local anesthetics, watch closely for progression to seizures and then cardiovascular collapse (arrhythmias). Have 20% lipid emulsion ready — the definitive antidote — and remember propofol is not an acceptable substitute.

Drugs Used for Pain Management

Topicals

The appeal of topicals is efficacy without the systemic side-effect burden of an oral drug — though absorption and effectiveness are limited by how well the drug reaches the site of pain.

Topical NSAIDs

  • Indicated for knee and hand OA — should be considered first for knee OA, ahead of systemic NSAIDs, because of limited systemic AEs
  • MOA: local inhibition of COX-2 enzymes (proposed)
  • AEs: pruritus, burning, pain, rash — still carry some of the same systemic risks as oral NSAIDs, just less
  • Not effective for back pain — can't reach the joint/pain source at depth

Diclofenac Gel 1%

Voltaren

Diclofenac Patch 1.3%

Flector

Diclofenac Solution 1.5%

Pennsaid

Capsaicin

  • Topical preparation isolated from hot peppers; placebo-controlled trials show significant pain relief when applied over affected joints
  • 2nd-line for knee OA; not recommended for hand OA
  • MOA: binds the TRPV1 receptor (vanilloid/capsaicin receptor), depleting substance P from nociceptive nerve fibers and decreasing pain transmission
  • AEs: burning, stinging, erythema — can take up to two weeks for full effect
🔑 Patient counseling matters

Avoid contact with eyes, mouth, or mucous membranes; wash hands thoroughly after application (unless hands are the treatment area); avoid heat exposure (hot showers, sun, heating pads) to the treated area, which can intensify the burning sensation.

Menthol

  • MOA: activates TRPA1 and TRPM8 (the cold-sensing channel) — initial stimulation of nociception followed by desensitization, producing a cooling sensation then reduced pain signaling
  • Combined with methyl salicylate, camphor, lidocaine, and other counterirritants
  • Menthol alone: Biofreeze, ActivICE. Menthol + methyl salicylate (an NSAID): Icy Hot, Bengay
  • Indications: musculoskeletal pain (not low back), pharyngitis, herpes labialis
☐ Topicals in Pregnancy

Diclofenac and methyl salicylate do undergo systemic absorption (blood levels are much lower than oral, but the drug still carries the same warnings as oral NSAIDs — minimize use 20–28 weeks, avoid after 28 weeks). Capsaicin has limited systemic absorption with no expected fetal transfer. Menthol has limited systemic absorption and is considered safe. Anesthetic lozenges/sprays (dyclonine, phenol, menthol, benzocaine) all appear safe.

Q: Why might a topical NSAID be a reasonable first choice for knee osteoarthritis but a poor choice for chronic low back pain?

Answer

The knee joint is superficial, so a topical NSAID can achieve locally therapeutic concentrations with minimal systemic absorption. The structures generating low back pain sit much deeper, so the drug can't reach an adequate concentration at the source — efficacy drops off even though the systemic-AE advantage remains.

PLO 3
PLO 5

Drugs Used for Pain Management

Antispasmodic Drugs

Also called centrally-active muscle relaxants or spasmolytics. They prevent use-related minor muscle spasms — indicated for low back pain, fibromyalgia, tension headaches, and myofascial pain syndrome. Despite being among the top 200 drugs dispensed, they are not recommended as first-line therapy — APAP and NSAIDs remain the drugs of choice, with antispasmodics used as adjuncts to physical therapy.

Cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril)

CNS muscle relaxant — most evidence for efficacy

Structurally related to TCAs — 5-HT2 receptor antagonist, muscarinic receptor antagonist, weak SERT/NET blockade, α1/α2 and H1 antagonism (noncompetitive). May decrease excitability of α/γ-motor neurons. AEs are largely anticholinergic: tachycardia, hypotension, drowsiness, xerostomia, urinary retention, ↑ intraocular pressure. CIs: recent MI, arrhythmias, glaucoma.

Methocarbamol (Robaxin)

Unknown MOA — general CNS depressant

AEs: black, brown, or green urine (harmless but alarming if unexpected); lightheadedness, dizziness, drowsiness.

Tizanidine (Zanaflex)

α2-adrenergic agonist — presynaptic, spinal

Inhibits spinal motor neurons (also used as an anti-spasticity agent). AEs: QT prolongation, dose-related hypotension, dizziness, xerostomia, hepatotoxicity. Has 1/10–1/50 the BP-lowering effect of clonidine; abrupt discontinuation causes withdrawal/rebound hypertension — taper.

⚠️ Evidence quality is weak

Studies of antispasmodics are generally poorly designed: inadequate randomization, no allocation concealment, no intention-to-treat analysis, incomplete compliance reporting. They appear roughly equivalent to NSAIDs for acute low back pain but show little evidence of effectiveness in chronic low back pain. It's unclear how much benefit comes from actual muscle relaxation vs. simple sedation. Combining an antispasmodic with an NSAID does show increased efficacy over either agent alone.

⚠️ Safety & Pregnancy

Sedation — caution with driving/heavy machinery; additive effects with alcohol/other sedative-hypnotics; caution in the elderly. Pregnancy — not recommended: methocarbamol has reported fetal abnormalities; cyclobenzaprine increases neural tube defect risk (avoid in the 1st trimester); tizanidine has limited data.

Q: A patient with acute low back pain and prominent muscle spasms has already tried an NSAID with partial relief. What's a reasonable next addition, and what should you specifically avoid?

Answer

Adding cyclobenzaprine (the antispasmodic with the most evidence) to the NSAID is reasonable — the combination shows better efficacy than either alone. Avoid carisoprodol (Soma), benzodiazepines, and meprobamate given their high abuse potential and lack of superior evidence for low back pain.

PLO 7

Pharmacological Management of Pain

Acute Pain Management

General Acute Pain — Stepwise Approach

  1. Mild-to-moderate painAPAP and oral NSAIDs — inflammatory pain responds better to NSAIDs.
  2. Moderate painOral NSAIDs — more effective than APAP, and as effective (or more) as oral opioids, opioid+APAP combos, or IV opioids.
  3. Moderate-to-severe painOral NSAID plus APAP may be as effective as an opioid plus APAP.
  4. Severe painImmediate-release opioid, lowest effective dose, shortest duration.
🚫 NOT preferred agents for acute pain
  • Mixed agonist-antagonist opioids — pain relief limited by a dose ceiling
  • Codeine — toxicity/efficacy affected by CYP2D6 variation
  • Fentanyl patches — never for acute pain
  • Gabapentinoids — growing evidence that benefit is marginal and doesn't outweigh the risk (CNS depression)
  • Antispasmodics — no role in generalized pain; only modest benefit combined with an NSAID for muscle-spasm-associated acute low back pain
  • Suzetrigine — no advantage over APAP/NSAIDs
  • Tramadol — an opioid with added risk (seizures, serotonin syndrome) and CYP2D6-dependent efficacy

Acute Pain During Pregnancy & Lactation

Mild-to-Moderate

APAP is safe as directed and preferred. NSAIDs reasonable ≤20 weeks if APAP ineffective, or short-term (≤48 h) at 20–28 weeks. Use an opioid instead beyond 28 weeks.

Moderate-to-Severe

NSAID (if appropriate per gestational age) alone or plus APAP, or an opioid at the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration — weigh risk vs. benefit each time.

Acute Non-Low Back Musculoskeletal Pain

Nonpharmacologic first: PRICE (different from low back pain, where staying active is preferred):

🛡️

Protection

🛌

Rest

🧊

Ice

(avoid heat)

🩹

Compression

⬆️

Elevation

  • Preferred: topical NSAIDs with or without menthol — the only intervention shown to improve all outcomes with the least risk of harm
  • Alternative: oral NSAIDs (if appropriate) or APAP
  • Recommend against opioids, including tramadol — significant AEs and risk of long-term addiction/overdose with no added benefit over an NSAID for musculoskeletal pain

Acute Low Back Pain

  1. Oral NSAIDs (first-line DOC)APAP may be no more effective than placebo, but worth trying if an NSAID can't be used.
  2. Antispasmodics (second-line)Cyclobenzaprine is reasonable first choice; not shown to be more effective than NSAIDs/APAP, but consider with prominent muscle spasms. Avoid baclofen/dantrolene (lack of evidence) and benzodiazepines/carisoprodol/meprobamate (abuse potential).
  3. Tramadol (third-line)Only when first- and second-line agents are ineffective or contraindicated. Lowest effective dose, shortest duration (<3 days).
✅ Pregnancy — Acute Low Back Pain

APAP first. Short course of NSAIDs if APAP ineffective (respecting the same gestational-age criteria as above). Muscle relaxants are not recommended during pregnancy.

Q: A pregnant patient at 32 weeks gestation has acute non-low-back musculoskeletal pain from a minor fall. Is a topical NSAID an acceptable choice?

Answer

Generally no — although topical NSAIDs have lower systemic exposure, diclofenac and methyl salicylate still undergo systemic absorption and carry the same warnings as oral NSAIDs (including risk of ductus arteriosus closure after 30 weeks). At 32 weeks, an opioid or non-pharmacologic measures (PRICE) would be preferred over an NSAID, topical or oral.

PLO 6
PLO 7

Pharmacological Management of Pain

Obstetric Pain Management

Labor and delivery analgesia today most commonly relies on neuraxial anesthesia — combining a local anesthetic with an opioid so that both can be used at a lower, less toxic dose while maintaining effective analgesia.

✅ Preferred combination

Bupivacaine + fentanyl are the expert-opinion drugs of choice. Ropivacaine + sufentanil are reasonable alternatives. Lidocaine is rarely used (short duration of action, higher degree of motor block). Opioids improve analgesia and provide more rapid onset compared to LA alone.

By minimizing the total dose of each drug through combination, neuraxial technique achieves several favorable effects at once:

Minimize Motor Block

Mom can move and push effectively when the time comes.

Avoid Hypotension

Both LA and opioid alone can cause hypotension — combining lowers each dose.

Minimize Placental Transfer

Less drug crossing to the fetus than with either agent alone at a full dose.

Reduce LAST Risk

Lower LA dose needed for effective analgesia.

Neuraxial anesthesia techniques — epidural, spinal, combined spinal-epidural (CSE)/dural puncture epidural (DPE), and continuous spinal

TechniqueOnsetEffect / DurationFlexibility
Spinal (single shot)QuickestMost reliable block; duration depends on drug/dose; lowest rate of pain during cesarean deliveryNo titration or reinjection possible
Epidural (via catheter)Not quickIncremental dosing required; block may be patchy, one-sided, or sacral-sparing; highest rate of pain during cesarean deliveryCatheter allows incremental/repeated dosing; usable for labor analgesia, cesarean anesthesia, and postop pain
Dural puncture epidural (DPE)Not quickSimilar to epidural but less patchy/one-sided/sacral-sparing than epidural aloneSame as epidural; confirms needle position via CSF
Combined spinal-epidural (CSE)Can be quickSpinal dose can be low, followed by epidural catheter placement; block less reliable than spinal alone but more effective than DPEEpidural catheter allows incremental/continuous/repeated dosing
Continuous spinal (intrathecal catheter)QuickAllows small incremental titrationIncremental/continuous/repeated dosing; risk of postdural puncture headache
🔑 Which technique is favored today?

CSE is increasingly the preferred technique for uncomplicated labor — it combines the rapid, dense onset of a spinal dose with the flexibility of an epidural catheter for the remainder of labor (or conversion to cesarean anesthesia).

Q: Why is lidocaine rarely chosen for labor epidural analgesia, even though it's the most versatile local anesthetic overall?

Answer

Lidocaine's short duration of action would require frequent redosing during a prolonged labor, and it produces a higher degree of motor block than bupivacaine or ropivacaine — undesirable when the goal is to preserve the mother's ability to move and push.

PLO 6
PLO 7

Pharmacological Management of Pain

Chronic Pain Management

Chronic low back pain, neuropathic pain, and osteoarthritis are the three chronic pain categories covered. The consistent theme: opioids are essentially never first-line for chronic noncancer pain, and the second/third-line options shift toward antidepressants and gabapentinoids rather than sedating muscle relaxants.

Chronic Low Back Pain

  1. NSAIDs (first-line)Carry even more cumulative risk with chronic use — reassess appropriateness regularly. Non-pharmacologic measures are usually the best overall approach.
  2. SNRIs (second-line)Duloxetine preferred; other SNRIs may help but with less data. TCAs and SSRIs are not recommended for chronic low back pain given their toxicity burden without added benefit.
  3. Third-lineGabapentinoids and antispasmodics are not recommended. Opioids should be avoided in most patients and are not first-line or recommended for any type of chronic noncancer pain.
🔑 Topicals have no role here

Topical NSAIDs can't reach the depth of the structures generating chronic low back pain — reserve topicals for superficial joints like the knee or hand.

Neuropathic Pain

LineAgents
PreferredTCAs (amitriptyline, nortriptyline, desipramine); SNRIs (duloxetine, venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine); gabapentinoids (gabapentin, pregabalin); carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine specifically for trigeminal neuralgia
If systemic agents are contraindicatedTopical lidocaine patch or capsaicin cream (small, confined areas only)
Third-lineOpioids (tramadol, tapentadol), SSRIs

Preferred agents are based largely on data from postherpetic neuralgia and diabetic neuropathy trials.

Postherpetic neuralgia treatment algorithm — first-line agent depends on whether pain is constant/burning (favor TCA) or brief/electric (favor gabapentinoid)

✅ The flip rule

If the first-choice class (TCA for constant/burning pain, gabapentinoid for lancinating/electric pain) fails or isn't tolerated, flip to the other class before moving further down the algorithm. Refractory symptoms ≥12 months, or preference for continued oral therapy, determines whether the next step is a second-line oral add/switch or referral for procedural options (epidural/intercostal glucocorticoid injection, high-concentration capsaicin, botulinum toxin, neuromodulation).

Chronic Pain in Pregnancy

Chronic Primary Pain

Consider antidepressants (amitriptyline, duloxetine, SSRIs). APAP, NSAIDs, opioids, AEDs, and gabapentinoids are not recommended for sustained chronic use in pregnancy.

Neuropathic / Cancer Pain

Neuropathic: duloxetine, amitriptyline, or gabapentinoids — same general approach as non-pregnant patients. Cancer pain: judicious use of opioids.

⚠️ Osteoarthritis in Pregnancy

APAP is safe. Aspirin (salicylates) is not recommended in pregnancy or lactation — risk of hemorrhage, prolonged labor, and perinatal mortality (note: low-dose aspirin for pre-eclampsia prevention is a separate, considered-safe indication). NSAIDs follow the same gestational-age criteria described in the NSAIDs in Pregnancy section.

🔑 Clinical vignette strategy

When a vignette could be either acute or chronic pain: look specifically for information that rules an NSAID in or out (pregnancy, CV disease, GI bleed history) — that's usually the detail the question is testing. And don't add information that isn't in the case: if pregnancy status, cardiovascular history, or GI history isn't mentioned, treat it as absent rather than assuming it to make an answer choice fit.

Q: A patient with chronic low back pain has failed an NSAID trial. Their PMH includes major depression. What's the most logical next step?

Answer

Duloxetine — it's the preferred second-line SNRI for chronic low back pain, and it doubles as treatment for the patient's depression. This is a good example of choosing an agent that addresses two problems at once, which vignettes often hint at through the past medical history.
